title: Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy become Novartis
what: The merger of Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy, announced on 7 March as the largest corporate merger ever, is being completed: Sandoz shares, last traded at 1,516 francs on 29 November, are exchanged for shares of the new Novartis. Ciba-Geigy's chairman Alex Krauer is chairman and Sandoz's Daniel Vasella chief executive.
why: The merger beat from the Novartis side: holders of Sandoz in the game become Novartis holders at the November prices.

title: Novartis opens for business
what: Novartis began operations on 20 December, formed from Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy in Basel. It makes medicines, crop protection products and seeds, and nutrition products such as Gerber baby food and Ovomaltine, and is expected to be the second-biggest drug company in the world after Glaxo Wellcome. Its registered share closed the year at 1,533 francs in Zurich.
why: The listing beat: why buy it? The second-biggest drug company in the world after Glaxo Wellcome, with Sandoz's transplant drugs and Ciba-Geigy's medicines under one roof, run by the Sandoz pharma chief Daniel Vasella.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novartis (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandoz (read 2026-10-03); NZZ of 3 Jan 1997 in data/manual/raw/nzz-notes-1995-1998.md (read 2026-10-03); data/src/profiles.ts

title: Swiss blue chips on a record run
what: Swiss shares set records in June; on 30 June the NZZ reported that the record run of the previous week had paused, after speculative gains in blue chips. Novartis's registered share closed June at 2,334 francs, against 1,920 at the end of May.
why: A 22% rise in francs in one month (18% in dollars, as the franc weakened). No Novartis-specific news was found; the beat ties the move to the 1997 Swiss boom, which is only part of the story.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 July 1997, p. 35 ('Abkühlung des Schweizer Aktienmarktes'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1997-07-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03); data/manual/raw/nzz-readings-1995-1998.csv

title: Syngenta is born; Novartis is now pure healthcare
what: Syngenta, the farm-chemicals and seeds company combining the agribusiness of Novartis and AstraZeneca, started on 13 November, based in Basel. Novartis shareholders received Syngenta shares. Novartis now makes only medicines, including low-priced copies of drugs whose patents have expired, and nutrition products.
why: The first of three big separations (Syngenta 2000, Alcon 2019, Sandoz 2023) that turn Novartis into a pure drug company.

title: Glivec: a cancer pill approved in record time
what: The US Food and Drug Administration approved Novartis's imatinib, sold as Gleevec in the US and Glivec elsewhere, for a form of leukaemia, only two and a half years after the application. Time magazine put it on its cover as a new weapon against cancer. It will cost about $30,000 a year.
why: The defining drug of the Vasella years: by 2012 it brings in $4.7 billion a year.

title: Generics united under the Sandoz name
what: This year Novartis organised all its generic drug businesses into one division under the old name Sandoz.
why: The Sandoz name returns as Novartis's generics arm, the business it spins off twenty years later. Year-end summary.

title: Novartis buys Hexal and Eon Labs
what: This year Novartis bought Hexal, one of Germany's leading generic drug makers, and the American generics company Eon Labs for $8.29 billion. Its Sandoz division is now the second-largest generics group in the world.
why: Vasella's bet on a two-legged strategy, patented drugs plus generics. Month not confirmed, hence a year-end summary.

title: Novartis sells Gerber to Nestlé
what: Novartis agreed in April to sell the American baby food maker Gerber to Nestlé for $5.5 billion. Nestlé is also buying Novartis's medical nutrition business for $2.5 billion.
why: The last of Sandoz's food businesses goes; Sandoz paid $3.7 billion for Gerber in 1994.

title: Novartis buys a quarter of Alcon from Nestlé
what: Novartis has bought about 25% of the eye-care company Alcon of Fort Worth, Texas, from Nestlé, which still owns the majority.
why: The first step of the Alcon story, which ends with the spin-off of 2019. Novartis rose 8% in July (11% in francs).

title: The market keeps sinking
what: Stocks fell again in February, the S&P 500 by 11%, as the banking crisis deepened. Novartis fell with the market.
why: The bottom of Novartis's worst stretch in the game, -40% from October 2006 to February 2009; the market low follows on 6 March. [Lookahead review: the March 2009 low was not known in February.]

title: The recovery reaches the drug makers
what: Stock markets extended their recovery from the March low; the S&P 500 rose 7% in July. Novartis rose 11% in francs.
why: Part of the general recovery; Novartis's own second-quarter results that month may have helped but were not checked in a source.

title: Novartis bids for all of Alcon; Jimenez takes over
what: On 4 January Novartis agreed to buy Nestlé's remaining majority of Alcon, part of a $39.3 billion offer for the whole company. Daniel Vasella handed the job of chief executive to Joseph Jimenez and stays chairman.
why: Alcon costs Novartis about $60 billion in all; Jimenez cuts costs hard. Both halves of the Vasella legacy, the size and the price, meet here.

title: The franc is capped at 1.20 per euro
what: On 6 September the Swiss National Bank set a minimum rate of 1.20 francs per euro and said it would buy foreign currency in unlimited quantities. The franc fell about 11% against the dollar in September, while Novartis shares rose about 8% in francs.
why: A currency lesson: up in francs, down 4% in the game's dollar prices.

title: Vasella leaves with a golden handshake
what: Daniel Vasella retired as chairman of Novartis in February after 17 years at the top. His departure package, reported at about $78 million including a payment for not working for competitors, caused an uproar in Switzerland weeks before a national vote on executive pay.
why: The end of the Vasella years; Novartis shares had lagged the industry during his tenure, according to Wikipedia.

title: Swiss voters back the initiative against 'rip-off salaries'
what: On 3 March Swiss voters approved Thomas Minder's initiative against excessive executive pay with 67.9% of the vote. The campaign drew particular attention to payouts at Novartis and the big banks.
why: A Swiss political beat with a Novartis face; no effect on the share price.

title: Asset swap with GlaxoSmithKline
what: Novartis announced in April that it will buy GlaxoSmithKline's cancer drug business for $16 billion and sell its vaccines business to GSK for $7.1 billion; the two also plan a joint venture in consumer health products.
why: Jimenez narrows Novartis to fewer, stronger businesses; the consumer stake is sold to GSK for $13 billion in 2018.

title: The franc floor is scrapped
what: On 15 January the Swiss National Bank abandoned its minimum rate of 1.20 francs per euro without warning; the franc closed 23% higher against the euro and 21% higher against the dollar that day. Swiss shares fell in francs because exporters' foreign earnings are worth less.
why: Novartis lost about 2% in francs but gained 5% in dollars: the franc did the work.

title: Entresto approved for heart failure
what: The US Food and Drug Administration approved Novartis's Entresto (sacubitril/valsartan) for heart failure on 7 July under priority review. In the PARADIGM-HF trial, stopped early because of its benefit, cardiovascular death or hospital stays for heart failure hit 21.8% of patients, against 26.5% on the standard drug enalapril.
why: The big new drug of the Jimenez years.

title: Vas Narasimhan named next chief executive
what: Novartis named Vasant Narasimhan, its head of drug development and chief medical officer, to succeed Joseph Jimenez as chief executive in February. He is a 41-year-old American doctor who joined Novartis in 2005.
why: Narasimhan is the architect of 'pure-play medicines': Alcon and Sandoz spun off, the Roche stake sold.

title: Narasimhan takes over and apologises for Cohen payments
what: Vasant Narasimhan became chief executive on 1 February. Within weeks he apologised to employees after it emerged that Novartis had signed a $1.2 million one-year contract with the consulting firm of Michael Cohen, the personal lawyer of President Trump.
why: A rocky start for the CEO who reshapes Novartis.

title: Novartis buys AveXis for gene therapy
what: This year Novartis bought AveXis, a developer of gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, for $218 a share, $8.7 billion in total. Novartis also sold its stake in the consumer health joint venture to GlaxoSmithKline for $13 billion in March.
why: AveXis brings Zolgensma, one of the most expensive treatments in the world. Month of AveXis not confirmed, hence a year-end summary.

title: Alcon spun off
what: On 9 April Novartis completed the spin-off of its eye-care business Alcon: shareholders received Alcon shares, now listed on their own, and the new company is valued at about 28 billion francs. Novartis is now focused on medicines and generics.
why: Undoes the Alcon purchase of 2008-2011. Our price series is adjusted for the spin-off, so the game shows no drop.

title: Novartis buys The Medicines Company
what: In late November Novartis agreed to buy The Medicines Company for $9.7 billion, $85 a share. It is Novartis's second big purchase under Narasimhan after AveXis.
why: A bet on mass-market cardiology under Narasimhan.

title: Vaccine news lifts the market
what: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech reported that their COVID-19 vaccine prevented about 91% of symptomatic infections in a trial with over 40,000 people. Stock markets jumped: the S&P 500 rose 11% in November.
why: Novartis rose 16% in a month (15% in francs), riding the vaccine rally after a weak October; Novartis had no vaccine of its own.

title: Novartis gives up its third of Roche
what: This year Novartis gave up its holding of about a third of the shares of its Basel neighbour Roche.
why: Ends a long cross-holding between the two Basel rivals. Details of the sale were not confirmed in a source read, hence a soft year-end summary.

title: Sandoz to be spun off by the end of 2023
what: Novartis said in August that it will complete the separation of its generics business Sandoz into an independent company by the end of 2023. It had announced in 2018 that Sandoz would become a stand-alone unit.
why: The last step to a pure patented-medicines company; the name Sandoz becomes independent again.

title: Sandoz goes its own way
what: On 4 October Novartis completed the spin-off of Sandoz: shareholders received one Sandoz share for every five Novartis shares, and Sandoz now trades on the Swiss exchange, with an expected value of $18 to 25 billion. Its chief executive is Richard Saynor. Novartis now sells only patented medicines.
why: The company that began as a merger of Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy sheds the Sandoz name 27 years later. Our series is adjusted for the spin-off.

title: Buying growth: Avidity for $12 billion
what: This year Novartis agreed to buy Avidity Biosciences for about $12 billion, after Anthos Therapeutics ($925 million) and, last year, MorphoSys (EUR 2.7 billion). In the third quarter its sales rose 8% and operating income 24%.
why: Narasimhan uses the cash from the separations to buy new drugs. Month of the Avidity deal not confirmed, hence a year-end summary.

title: Fourth-quarter results and a strong month for the share
what: Novartis reported on 4 February that fourth-quarter sales rose 1% in dollars (down 1% at constant currencies) to $13.3 billion, with net income down 15%. The share rose strongly in February and reached a record.
why: The share rose 14% in February, but the published figures look weak; the cause of the rise was not found (see Unexplained moves). It fell back 11% in March.
